name: Battle of Mylae
intro: Off Mylae, on the north coast of Sicily, 260 BC. Rome’s new fleet faces Carthage, the greatest sea power of the age. You are the consul Gaius Duilius, with about 145 ships against perhaps 130.
debrief: In Polybius’s account, the Roman ships were fitted with the corvus, a boarding bridge with a spike. The Carthaginians, under Hannibal Gisco, attacked confidently and in poor order. The corvi pinned the first ships, and Roman marines took thirty of them, including the flagship; Hannibal escaped in a boat. When the rest tried to attack from the sides and stern, the swinging bridges met them there too. About fifty Carthaginian ships were lost. Duilius was honoured with a column decorated with the captured rams. The other choices are what-ifs.

win: Fifty Carthaginian ships are taken or sunk.
Rome wins its first battle at sea.
lose: The Carthaginians row round the clumsy ships.
Roman ships sink one after another.

decisions.title: A new kind of ship
decisions.text: Your ships are heavy and your crews new. The Carthaginians are the best seamen in the world. But your ships carry a new device: the corvus, a swinging bridge with a spike that can pin an enemy ship. You are the consul Gaius Duilius.

hint.text: Carthaginian crews ram and row away; they never fight hand to hand.

scout.text: Fit every ship with a corvus and fight as if on land.

choices.label: Fit every ship with the corvus

fx.text: Every ship carries a corvus, raised high on its mast, with marines ready to cross.

choices.label: Train the crews to ram like the Carthaginians

fx.text: The crews practise ramming, but they will never match Carthage at it.

choices.label: Avoid battle and raid the coast instead

fx.text: Carthage keeps command of the sea.

decisions.title: Off Mylae
decisions.text: The Carthaginian fleet under Hannibal Gisco comes on fast, in no particular order, sure of victory. They have never lost to Rome at sea.

scout.text: Let them come. Do not meet them halfway.

choices.label: Hold your line and let them come

fx.text: Your line waits, corvi raised. The Carthaginians row in, laughing at the strange masts.

choices.label: Charge them before they can form a line

fx.text: The two fleets meet in confusion.

decisions.title: The first ships close
decisions.text: The first thirty Carthaginian ships ram your front line.

hint.text: Their ships are now right against yours.

choices.label: Drop the corvi and board them

fx.text: The corvi crash down and spike the enemy decks. Roman marines pour across. Thirty ships are taken, Hannibal’s flagship among them; he escapes in a small boat.
Without a corvus, the marines fight to board.

choices.label: Back water and ram them in turn

fx.text: The Carthaginians are the better rowers.

choices.label: Keep the corvi raised and fire missiles

decisions.title: The second line
decisions.text: The rest of the Carthaginian fleet tries to come round your flanks and stern, where the corvus cannot reach.

hint.text: The corvus swings round in a full circle.

scout.text: Turn the bridges to meet them wherever they come.

choices.label: Swing the corvi round to meet them

fx.text: Wherever they come, the bridges swing round to meet them. Twenty more ships are taken or sunk.

choices.label: Form a circle so they cannot reach your sterns

fx.text: The Carthaginians cannot break in, but you take few ships.
The second line hits your sterns while you chase.

decisions.title: Victory at sea
decisions.text: The Carthaginian fleet is fleeing. Rome has won its first sea battle.

hint.text: The coast of Sicily lies open.

fx.text: You land and relieve Segesta, which Carthage was besieging. In Rome you are given a column decorated with the rams of the captured ships.
The fleet is not ready for the open sea.
